about: Spoken commentary for the universe stories (public/universe/stories/), one line per chapter, in the order of STORIES in stories.js. Each line starts just after its chapter opens; while it is heard, a chapter waits for its line to finish. tools/narration.py records the files and fills in 'dur' (seconds).

cues.text: Let's start close to home. The four planets nearest the Sun are made of rock, and the Earth is the biggest of them, just ahead of Venus.
Beyond Mars come the giants. Jupiter is eleven Earths wide. You could fit about thirteen hundred Earths inside it.
That red spot on Jupiter is a storm, watched since at least 1831. It's been shrinking, but the whole Earth would still fit inside it.
Saturn's rings stretch about two hundred and seventy thousand kilometres. Yet in most places, they're only about ten metres thick.
And the Sun? It's a hundred and nine times as wide as the Earth. More than a million Earths would fit inside it.
In 1990, Voyager 1 looked back from six billion kilometres away. And there we are: less than a single pixel. A pale blue dot.
Our nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is a red dwarf, not much wider than Jupiter. Most of the stars around us are small, cool red dwarfs like this.
Sirius, the brightest star in our sky, is a little wider than the Sun. Its tiny companion is a white dwarf, about the size of the Earth.
Arcturus and Aldebaran are old stars that have swollen into giants. In about five billion years, our Sun will swell like this too.
Rigel, in Orion, is a blue supergiant: young, hot, and about seventy-nine times as wide as the Sun. Stars like it burn out in just a few million years.
Betelgeuse is a red supergiant. Put it where the Sun is, and it would reach past the orbit of Mars. One day, both of these stars will explode.
This is one of the biggest stars we know: about fourteen hundred times as wide as the Sun. In our place, it would reach past Jupiter.
Here's every size at once, in three panels. Each dashed box is the whole of the panel before it. Go on, zoom in and take a closer look.
These are all the stars we know of within about twelve light years of the Sun. This is our neighbourhood.
The closest is Proxima Centauri, four point two light years away. Even Voyager 1 would need about seventy-five thousand years to get there.
Barnard's Star moves across our sky faster than any other star. It's getting closer, and it has at least four small planets.
Sirius looks so bright because it's close, just eight point six light years away, and it's about twenty-five times as bright as the Sun.
Some of our neighbours were only found recently: brown dwarfs, too small to shine like real stars. One of them is about as cold as a freezer.
This is our galaxy, the Milky Way, a hundred thousand light years across. The Sun takes about two hundred and thirty million years to go once around.
This little galaxy is being torn apart by ours. Its stars are stretched into a stream that loops right around the Milky Way.
The Magellanic Clouds are two small galaxies close to ours. From the southern hemisphere, you can see them with your own eyes.
Andromeda is two and a half million light years away. The light we see from it left before our species even existed.
And Andromeda is heading our way. Will the two galaxies merge? Astronomers now put the chance at about one in two, within ten billion years.
Together, these galaxies make up the Local Group: a family of more than eighty, and we're still finding new ones.
Light is the fastest thing there is. Even so, sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach us.
To reach Neptune, the outermost planet, sunlight needs about four hours.
Now zoom out to the nearest star, and the whole solar system shrinks to a dot.
Keep going, and you get the Milky Way. If you counted one star a second, a hundred billion of them would take you more than three thousand years.
Hubble stared at a tiny patch of sky that looked empty. It found about ten thousand galaxies.
And the whole universe we can see? Up to two trillion galaxies, and more stars than there are grains of sand on all the Earth's beaches.
Until 1992, we didn't know of a single planet outside our solar system. Now we know more than six thousand. Most stars have planets.
Most are found like this: a planet passes in front of its star, and the star's light dips, just a tiny bit.
A planet also makes its star wobble. In 1995, that wobble revealed a giant planet with a year of just four days.
Trappist-1 has seven planets about the size of the Earth, and three of them could have liquid water.
This planet circles two stars at once. Stand on it, and you'd see two sunsets.
And on this planet, one side is hot enough to boil iron. It might even rain iron on the cooler side.
